HIGH Accessibility CONFIRMED · 95% SMALL fix

Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds

7 pages 63 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 1.4.3 priority 160

Ensure the contrast between foreground and background colors meets WCAG 2 AA minimum contrast ratio thresholds

How we know measured evidence
axe rule color-contrast axe-core
Impact serious axe-core
Failing elements on this page 4 axe-core
WCAG criteria 1.4.3 axe-core rule tags
Why this matters interpretation

This is a failure of WCAG success criterion 1.4.3. Ensure the contrast between foreground and background colors meets WCAG 2 AA minimum contrast ratio thresholds Users relying on assistive technology are affected directly; the failure is invisible to sighted mouse users, which is why it persists.

Impact: Users with low vision, colour vision deficiency, or anyone reading on a phone in daylight cannot reliably read this text.

Recommended fix small effort

Increase the contrast between the text and its background to at least 4.5:1 for body text (3:1 for text at 18pt/14pt-bold or larger). Adjusting the text colour is usually less disruptive than changing the background.

Technical detail 
Rule: color-contrast (serious impact)
Reference: https://dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.13/color-contrast?application=axeAPI

HIGH Accessibility CONFIRMED · 95% TRIVIAL fix

Interactive controls have no accessible name

1 page 6 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value priority 110

6 visible interactive element(s) expose no accessible name.

How we know measured evidence
Unnamed controls 6 Accessible-name computation
#news-section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > button:nth-of-type(1) <button> DOM extraction
#news-section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > button:nth-of-type(2) <button> DOM extraction
div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(1) <button> DOM extraction
div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(2) <button> DOM extraction
div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(3) <button> DOM extraction
Why this matters interpretation

These are almost always icon-only controls — a hamburger menu, a close button, a search icon — where the icon is rendered as an SVG or a background image with no text alternative. Sighted users read the icon; assistive technology has nothing to read.

Impact: A screen reader announces these as "button" or "link" with no name. In a page with several, the user cannot distinguish between them at all.

Recommended fix trivial effort

Add `aria-label` describing the action ("Close dialog", "Open navigation menu", "Search"), or include visually-hidden text inside the control. For SVG icons, `<title>` inside the SVG plus `role="img"` also works.

"View All Organizations" triggers a failing request (network error)

2 pages 7 occurrences priority 103

Clicking "View All Organizations" issued a request to /api/dashboard/summary which failed (net::ERR_ABORTED).

How we know measured evidence
Control View All Organizations Computed accessible name
Request GET https://ngo-ups3.onrender.com/api/dashboard/summary Chromium network stack
Status net::ERR_ABORTED Chromium network stack
Navigation occurred yes Page URL before/after click
DOM mutations after click 402 MutationObserver
Why this matters interpretation

The request the control depends on did not succeed, so the action it represents did not complete.

Impact: The user journey that runs through this control is broken. If the UI does not surface the failure, users will believe the action succeeded — which is worse than an obvious error.

Recommended fix medium effort

Confirm /api/dashboard/summary is the correct endpoint and that the request shape matches what the server expects. Add explicit error handling on the client.

How to reproduce
  1. Open https://www.impactbridge.forum/ with the DevTools Network panel recording
  2. Click "View All Organizations"
  3. Observe GET /api/dashboard/summary returning net::ERR_ABORTED

Environment: DESKTOP viewport, FAST network profile

Buttons must have discernible text

1 page 6 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 4.1.2 priority 98

Ensure buttons have discernible text

How we know measured evidence
axe rule button-name axe-core
Impact critical axe-core
Failing elements on this page 6 axe-core
WCAG criteria 4.1.2 axe-core rule tags
Why this matters interpretation

This is a failure of WCAG success criterion 4.1.2. Ensure buttons have discernible text Users relying on assistive technology are affected directly; the failure is invisible to sighted mouse users, which is why it persists.

Impact: The control announces with no name, so a screen reader user has no way to know what activating it will do. In a list of links this makes the page unnavigable.

Recommended fix small effort

Give the button an accessible name via its text content, `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby`. Icon-only buttons need this without exception.

Technical detail 
Rule: button-name (critical impact)
Reference: https://dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.13/button-name?application=axeAPI

Why this matters interpretation

Without a long `max-age`, the browser must revalidate or re-download these assets on every visit. For fingerprinted build outputs — filenames containing a content hash — this is pure waste: the content can never change under a given URL, so it is safe to cache indefinitely.

Impact: Repeat visitors re-download assets that have not changed, making the second visit almost as slow as the first and consuming bandwidth unnecessarily.

Recommended fix small effort

Serve fingerprinted assets with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. For assets whose URL is stable across deploys, use a shorter max-age with `stale-while-revalidate` so the browser can serve instantly while refreshing in the background.

No Content-Security-Policy header

7 pages 7 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 80

The `content-security-policy` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header content-security-policy HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

CSP is the primary defence against cross-site scripting. It tells the browser which sources are allowed to execute script, so that even if an attacker manages to inject a `<script>` tag, the browser refuses to run it. Without a policy, any successful injection executes with full privileges.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Deploy a Content-Security-Policy. Start in report-only mode (`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`) with a collection endpoint so you can see what would break before enforcing, then tighten toward `default-src 'self'` with explicit allowances.

MEDIUM Security CONFIRMED · 95% SMALL fix

No Strict-Transport-Security header

7 pages 7 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 80

The `strict-transport-security` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header strict-transport-security HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

HSTS instructs the browser to use HTTPS for this host for a stated period, without waiting for a redirect. It closes the window in which a first plain-http request can be intercepted and downgraded — the classic coffee-shop attack.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`. Roll out with a short max-age first and confirm every subdomain serves HTTPS correctly before extending it, because the directive is not easily reversible in browsers that have cached it.

Multiple pages share the same title

4 pages 4 occurrences priority 70

2 title(s) are used by more than one page, affecting 4 pages in total.

How we know measured evidence

ImpactBridge | Connect NGOs, Volunteers, Donors & Ethical Co… [truncated 6 chars] 2 pages Cross-page comparison
ImpactBridge | Unite for Impact 2 pages Cross-page comparison
Why this matters interpretation

Titles are how search engines and users tell pages apart. When several pages carry the same title, search engines have difficulty deciding which is the best result for a query, and users looking at a list of results or browser tabs cannot distinguish them. This pattern almost always means a template is emitting a static title instead of interpolating page-specific content.

Impact: Weakened relevance signals and worse search presentation across a group of pages.

Recommended fix small effort

Make each title unique by interpolating page-specific content into the template — the product name, article headline, or category, plus the site name.

Server response time (TTFB) is 927 ms

1 page 1 occurrence priority 43

The browser waited 927 ms for the first byte of the HTML document.

How we know measured evidence
TTFB 927 ms Navigation Timing API (responseStart)
Recommended threshold 800 ms web.dev
Cache-Control on document no-store Response headers
Server cloudflare Response headers
Why this matters interpretation

TTFB is the time from navigation start until the first byte of HTML arrives. It is composed of DNS, connection setup, TLS, request travel, server processing, and response travel — none of which frontend code can influence. Because every other metric on the page starts counting from here, TTFB sets a floor that no amount of asset optimisation can go below.

Impact: Every visitor waits this long before anything at all can render. It is the single largest fixed cost in the page load and it affects first-time and returning visitors alike.

Recommended fix medium effort

Add full-page or fragment caching at the origin so repeat requests are not recomputed, and put a CDN in front so the response is served from a point of presence near the user.

Main thread blocked for 220 ms during load

1 page 1 occurrence priority 38

Total Blocking Time is 220 ms across 3 long task(s), against a 200ms budget.

How we know measured evidence
Total Blocking Time 220 ms PerformanceObserver (longtask), TBT definition
Long tasks (>50 ms) 3 PerformanceObserver (longtask)
Longest single task 225 ms PerformanceObserver (longtask)
Why this matters interpretation

The browser runs JavaScript on the same thread that handles clicks, scrolling, and rendering. Any task longer than 50 ms makes the page unresponsive for its duration — a click during that window is queued, not dropped, so the user experiences a delay rather than a failure. Total Blocking Time sums the portion of each long task beyond 50 ms, which is why it maps closely to perceived jank.

Impact: Clicks and taps feel laggy or unresponsive during load. On lower-powered devices — where CPU is several times slower than a development machine — these durations multiply.

Recommended fix large effort

Take a DevTools performance profile and look at the longest tasks first. Common fixes: defer non-critical third-party scripts until after load, break large synchronous work into chunks with `scheduler.yield()` or `setTimeout`, and move heavy computation into a Web Worker.

No X-Content-Type-Options header

7 pages 7 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 32

The `x-content-type-options` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header x-content-type-options HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Without `nosniff`, browsers may ignore the declared Content-Type and guess based on content. A user-uploaded file served as text/plain but containing HTML can then be interpreted as HTML and execute script.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. It has essentially no compatibility risk.

No Referrer-Policy header

7 pages 7 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 32

The `referrer-policy` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header referrer-policy HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Without an explicit policy, browsers send the full URL of the current page — path and query string included — to third-party resources. Where URLs contain identifiers, reset tokens, or search terms, that is a quiet data leak to every analytics and ad domain on the page.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`. This keeps full referrer information for same-origin navigation while sending only the origin to third parties.

Why this matters interpretation

Without `X-Frame-Options` or a CSP `frame-ancestors` directive, the page can be embedded in an invisible iframe on an attacker's site and overlaid with decoy controls, so a user believes they are clicking one thing while actually clicking another on your site.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, or preferably the modern equivalent `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'`.

How we know measured evidence
Anchors without a destination 1 DOM extraction

Why this matters interpretation

An anchor is a navigation element. When it carries no destination it is usually being used as a button with a JavaScript handler attached. That works for mouse users but breaks middle-click, right-click "open in new tab", and keyboard activation semantics, and it announces incorrectly to screen readers.

Impact: Keyboard and assistive-technology users get a control that announces as a link but does not behave like one. Mouse users lose open-in-new-tab.

Cookies are missing security attributes

7 pages 7 occurrences OWASP A05:2021 — Security Misconfiguration priority 25

3 cookie(s) observed; 0 without Secure, 3 without HttpOnly, 3 without a restrictive SameSite.

How we know measured evidence
Cookies observed 3 CDP Network.getAllCookies
Missing Secure 0 Cookie attributes
Missing HttpOnly 3 Cookie attributes
Missing/None SameSite 3 Cookie attributes
Why this matters interpretation

`Secure` stops the cookie being sent over plain HTTP. `HttpOnly` stops JavaScript reading it, which is what limits the damage of an XSS flaw to actions rather than session theft. `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` stops it being attached to cross-site requests, which is the main structural defence against CSRF. We can observe which attributes are set but not what each cookie is used for — a missing HttpOnly on an analytics cookie is unremarkable, on a session cookie it is serious.

Impact: Where any of these cookies carries a session, the missing attributes translate directly into session theft via XSS, session leakage over HTTP, or CSRF.

Recommended fix small effort

Set `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` on every session and authentication cookie. Where a cookie must be readable by client-side script, confirm that is genuinely required — it usually is not.

No XML sitemap found

1 page 1 occurrence priority 20

No sitemap was found at /sitemap.xml, /sitemap_index.xml, or referenced from robots.txt.

How we know measured evidence
sitemap.xml not found HTTP probe
Referenced in robots.txt no robots.txt parse
Why this matters interpretation

A sitemap gives search engines an explicit list of URLs to crawl along with change frequency hints. Without one, crawlers rely entirely on following links — so pages that are poorly linked internally, or newly published, are discovered slowly or not at all.

Impact: Slower discovery and indexing of new or deeply-nested pages.

Recommended fix small effort

Generate an XML sitemap and reference it from robots.txt with a `Sitemap:` directive. Most frameworks and CMSs can produce one automatically.

Technical detail 
Probed /sitemap.xml and /sitemap_index.xml; neither returned a parseable sitemap.

No Permissions-Policy header

7 pages 7 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 8

The `permissions-policy` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header permissions-policy HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Permissions-Policy lets a site declare which powerful browser features (camera, microphone, geolocation, payment) may be used, including by embedded third-party frames. Without it, any embedded content can request those permissions in the site's name.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add a Permissions-Policy disabling features the site does not use, e.g. `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`.

Method & Scope

What was tested

  • 7 page(s) loaded in a real Chromium browser at desktop viewport
  • 236 network request(s) observed, 9.27 MB transferred
  • 46 interactive control(s) clicked and observed
  • 5 link target(s) verified · 2 broken
  • 0 console error(s) and uncaught exception(s) captured
  • Accessibility scanned with axe-core against WCAG 2.1 A/AA and 2.2 AA

How to read this report

  • Measured facts are observations from the browser. They are not estimates.
  • Interpretation is our reasoning from those facts, and is labelled separately.
  • Confidence — CONFIRMED means we observed the failure directly; POSSIBLE means the evidence is suggestive but a benign explanation exists.
  • Priority combines severity, confidence, how much of the site is affected, and effort.
  • AI enrichment was not used for this audit — all findings and prose are rule-generated.

Limits of this audit

  • Black-box only — no source code, backend, or database access.
  • Security checks are passive: response headers and transport configuration observed during normal page loads. No active scanning or probing was performed.
  • Interaction testing deliberately skips anything that looks destructive (delete, purchase, logout, submit), so those paths are untested.
  • Pages behind authentication were not tested.
  • A single measurement per page — network timing varies between runs.
